title: Gram-Schmidt
body:
**Gram-Schmidt** turns any [[Basis]] into an [[Orthonormal Basis]] for the same space, one vector
at a time. The rule is a single sentence: *take the next vector and subtract off everything that
was already covered.*

$$
\mathbf{w}_k = \mathbf{v}_k - \sum_{i<k} (\mathbf{v}_k \cdot \mathbf{u}_i)\,\mathbf{u}_i,
\qquad \mathbf{u}_k = \frac{\mathbf{w}_k}{\|\mathbf{w}_k\|}
$$

The sum is the [[Projection]] of $\mathbf{v}_k$ onto the span of everything processed so far, so
$\mathbf{w}_k$ is the residual and is orthogonal to all of it by construction. Normalise, move on.

Two properties fall out and both get used:

- $\text{span}\{\mathbf{u}_1,\dots,\mathbf{u}_k\} = \text{span}\{\mathbf{v}_1,\dots,\mathbf{v}_k\}$
  at **every** step, not just at the end. The process is nested.
- $\mathbf{w}_k = \mathbf{0}$ exactly when $\mathbf{v}_k$ was already in the span of its
  predecessors, so Gram-Schmidt is also a dependence detector.

## Worked example

$\mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix}1\\1\\0\end{bmatrix}$,
$\mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix}1\\0\\1\end{bmatrix}$.

$$
\mathbf{u}_1 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\\0\end{bmatrix}
$$

$\mathbf{v}_2 \cdot \mathbf{u}_1 = 1/\sqrt2$, so

$$
\mathbf{w}_2 = \begin{bmatrix}1\\0\\1\end{bmatrix} - \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\cdot\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\\0\end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix}1/2\\-1/2\\1\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\mathbf{u}_2 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{3/2}}\begin{bmatrix}1/2\\-1/2\\1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Check $\mathbf{u}_1 \cdot \mathbf{u}_2 = 0$. Always check; it costs one dot product and catches
every arithmetic slip.

## QR decomposition

Bookkeeping the process gives a factorisation. If $A$ has the $\mathbf{v}_k$ as columns and $Q$
has the $\mathbf{u}_k$, then each $\mathbf{v}_k$ is a combination of $\mathbf{u}_1$ through
$\mathbf{u}_k$ only, so the coefficient matrix is upper triangular:

$$
A = QR, \qquad Q^TQ = I, \qquad R = Q^TA \text{ upper triangular}
$$

**QR is how [[Least Squares]] is actually solved.** Substituting into the normal equations,
$A^TA\mathbf{x} = A^T\mathbf{y}$ becomes $R\mathbf{x} = Q^T\mathbf{y}$, a triangular system solved
by back-substitution. That avoids ever forming $A^TA$, which squares the conditioning and is the
standard way to lose half your digits. The same factorisation drives the QR algorithm for
[[Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors|eigenvalues]], which is what library code runs instead of the
characteristic polynomial.

**Numerical caution:** classical Gram-Schmidt as written above loses orthogonality badly on
nearly dependent columns. Modified Gram-Schmidt (subtract each projection immediately rather than
summing first) is the same arithmetic in a better order, and Householder reflections are what
[[NumPy|`numpy.linalg.qr`]] actually uses. The formula is for understanding; the library is for
answers, the same distinction [[Matrix Inverse]] draws about solving systems.
